In recent time, after the present landscape had been carved on the rocks by streams, parts of the outcrops of the coal seams were ignited, perhaps by spontaneous combustion, lightning, forest fires, or grass fires. The intense heat of the burning coal partly fused and reddened the overlying rocks. Considerable distortion and disruption of the rocks occurred when they collapsed into the voids created by burning of the coal.
The present valley floors of the major streams contain sand, gravel, silt, and clay deposits that fill previous sharp incisions of the valleys. In East Sarpy Creek valley, at the northeast corner of Tract III, one drill hole penetrated 80 fee of alluvium and did not reach undisturbed strata. This earlier deepening of valleys is widespread in the Great Plains region. The alluvium of the valley floors constitute a source of limited quantities of ground water.
Economic Deposits
Coal - The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (1972) reports that about 17 billion tons of strippable coal lie within Rosebud, Custer, Powder River, Big Horn, and Treasure Counties. The major amount of this coal is of subbituminous and lignite rank and occurs in the Fort Union formation.
